paragraphs.source_en: Regarding the Round Head-like figures outside the main area, the circular shape of the head cannot be the only criteria for the attribution to this style since human figures of any period and place can logically be represented with a round head. Since the Round Heads are characterised for the elements which are not present in the Pastoral art, or at least not in the same context, I argue that these elements, as the fundamental characters of the Round Head culture, must also be present on other figures if they are to be attributed to this style.

paragraphs.source_en: Except for some rare elements, namely the half-moon and a similar posture of the body represented in Ennedi (Jelinek 2004: 166), a T-shaped object and body decoration found in the Tibesti (Scarpa Falce 2009), other regions do not seem to present the elements characteristic for the Round Heads in the Tassili, Algerian Tadrart and Acacus. This situation is likely to indicate that these elements were not equally important everywhere, which possibly indicates that they were not fundamental in the culture, rituals or ceremonies of all Central Saharan groups.

paragraphs.source_en: The Round Heads in the Tassili, Algerian Tadrart, Acacus and the Djado are concentrated in selected places. The sites and the paintings appear to make an inseparable unity; they seem to have been ritual places highlighted by a large number of ritual images. Now, if the Round Heads were also present in very distant regions it would imply that people creating this art travelled great distances across the Sahara in order to make their rituals or ceremonies in other places. However, large concentrations of Round Heads have only been found in the Tassili. The few and isolated Round Head-like figures documented in Jebel Uweinat, Ennedi and probably Tibesti may have been the work of local populations occupying these mountainous regions.
